extracted.intended_audience: researchers in computational humor, AI/NLP researchers and cognitive/linguistic scholars interested in formalizing incongruity-resolution theories of verbal jokes
extracted.subtask_description: Developing precise, computationally implementable accounts of incongruity-resolution theories of verbally expressed humour, especially the Surprise Disambiguation and Suls two-stage variants; identifying the processing capabilities and definitional subcomponents needed for interpretation. Targeted at building or evaluating systems that detect/interpret joke set-ups and punchlines and that determine what makes an incongruity humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity (general requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour involves incongruity — a clash, inconsistency, or something out of keeping — but the notion needs precise definition for modelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper notes dictionary senses and historical definitions (e.g. Beattie 1776); emphasises that many writers use different, imprecise senses. Requirement for any formal model: provide a clear, explicit account of what counts as 'incongruity' in verbal jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-Resolution (IR) process
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is created by a multi-stage process where an initial incongruity is created and then further information causes that incongruity to be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Shultz (1976) for heuristic value; resolution may be logical or a reinterpretation that makes the punchline less incongruous. The paper debates whether resolution is necessary in all cases and notes variants where resolution takes different forms (e.g. ambiguity disambiguation, cognitive-rule resolution). Examples: riddles (1),(2),(3),(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise disambiguation (SD) model
rubrics_metrics.description: Set-up has two interpretations (one OBVIOUS, one HIDDEN); punchline conflicts with the OBVIOUS interpretation but is compatible with the hidden one, producing surprise and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SD requires an ambiguous set-up; central entities are: the first (obvious) interpretation, the second (hidden) interpretation, and the meaning of the punchline. Relations of interest (OBVIOUSNESS, CONFLICT, COMPATIBILITY, COMPARISON, INAPPROPRIATENESS) are used to characterise SD jokes. Examples: classic riddle-style jokes and many SD-analysable jokes like (6),(7),(9),(10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suls' two-stage model
rubrics_metrics.description: The punchline creates an incongruity which then requires a cognitive rule to be found that makes the punchline follow from the set-up; if a suitable rule is found the result is HUMOUR, otherwise PUZZLEMENT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processing sketch: as text is read make predictions; while no conflict, continue; if input conflicts with predictions then if not ending => PUZZLEMENT; if ending => try to resolve via cognitive rule => no rule => PUZZLEMENT, rule found => HUMOUR. Does not require ambiguous set-up, so covers different joke subclasses (examples (5),(8),(14)).

rubrics_metrics.name: OBVIOUSNESS
rubrics_metrics.description: What makes one potential interpretation of the set-up more likely or salient to the audience than another (i.e. the OBVIOUS interpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper flags OBVIOUSNESS as a central research subproblem: models must account for accessibility/priority of interpretations (references: De Palma & Weiner on accessibility, Giora on markedness). OBVIOUSNESS may be implemented via statistics, semantic priming, or processing convenience; exact mechanism must be defined for any computational account.

rubrics_metrics.name: CONFLICT / COMPATIBILITY
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the punchline (or continuation) is incompatible (CONFLICT) or compatible (COMPATIBILITY) with the currently maintained interpretation of the set-up; degree of difficulty assimilating text that triggers search for alternative interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Needed both for detection of punchline (when assimilation fails) and as a candidate contributor to humour. Questions: how difficult must assimilation be to initiate reinterpretation, and how to use the text portion that caused reassessment to guide the search. CONFLICT may be between punchline and OBVIOUS interpretation or between punchline and a PREDICTED continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: COMPARISON (script opposition / contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: What it means for two interpretations to differ in an amusing way — the contrastive relationship (script opposition) between the initial and revised interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SSTH/Raskin emphasises COMPARISON as central; Giora's 'markedness' and other proposals attempt to formalise this. Model must distinguish mere difference from amusing contrast (e.g. quality, conceptual distance, semantic opposition). COMPARISON can be combined with CONFLICT and OBVIOUSNESS to characterise the humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: INAPPROPRIATENESS (absurdity/taboo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the hidden interpretation is inherently odd, eccentric, taboo, or socially inappropriate, contributing to amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes forms of incongruity: ABSURDITY (violates everyday logic) vs TABOO (violates social norms). Paper treats INAPPROPRIATENESS as a separate factor that can augment or substitute for COMPARISON in producing humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: PREDICTION / violated expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Role of audience predictions (expectations) derived from the set-up; humour may arise from violation of specific predictions at semantic, syntactic, or lexical levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suls and Shultz define incongruity as violation of expectations; the paper questions whether conflict with a specific predicted continuation is necessary. Prediction can be at multiple linguistic levels (semantic, syntactic, lexical), and modelling might use psycholinguistic notions (garden-pathing, priming) or probabilistic prediction to operationalise this.

rubrics_metrics.name: INTERPRETATION (granularity of meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification of what counts as an 'interpretation' — overall propositional meaning vs particular ways of expressing it (idioms, pragmatic status, phrasing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models must decide whether switches in idiomatic phrasing or pragmatic reading count as different interpretations for SD analyses (examples (11),(12),(13)). May require levels prior to idiom decoding or pragmatic layers in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyzing the set-up (processing capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system must extract a symbolic representation of the multi-sentence set-up, make at least some inferences, and select the most OBVIOUS interpretation (or compute multiple readings and rank them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is essentially a text-understanding module; when multiple interpretations exist the processor must identify (or compute and rank) the OBVIOUS one. Cultural knowledge may be required for some jokes (example: (11) relies on football knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predicting (processing capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system must be able to reason ahead to predict likely continuations (meanings and sometimes lexical items) from the set-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prediction supports the identification of violated expectations; useful levels include lexical/probabilistic predictions as well as higher-level semantic/situation predictions. Computational linguistics and psycholinguistics offer techniques for modeling such prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting the punchline (processing capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processor must identify where the punchline begins (one word, sentence, or sequence) by constructing a separate structure to compare with the meaning of the set-up and noticing non-assimilation or conflict with predicted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No explicit textual markers in general; detection strategies include noticing failure to assimilate into current interpretation (indicating potential punchline) or mismatch with a predicted continuation. Requires mechanisms for assimilation failure detection and for matching at the relevant linguistic level (semantic/lexical/syntactic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing the punchline / resolution (processing capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a detected punchline, the processor must find an interpretation that covers both set-up and punchline (by computing alternative readings or backtracking and selecting an alternative interpretation compatible with punchline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple readings were maintained earlier, select one that assimilates punchline; if only one reading initially maintained, backtracking is necessary. For conflicts with predicted material, reinterpretation of the prediction or set-up is required. Complexity of reasoning may affect humorousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing the humorous effect (evaluation metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The processor must assess the extent to which factors such as COMPARISON, INAPPROPRIATENESS, and CONFLICT are present to determine whether the result is humorous rather than merely a resolved misunderstanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper emphasises that delivery/detection steps are insufficient — a separate assessment stage must rate amusingness. This assessment may require quantifying degrees of COMPARISON, INAPPROPRIATENESS, CONFLICT, and their combinations, and may be theory-external (derived from independent psycholinguistic constructs) or theory-internal (special definitions for humour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing degrees and threshold conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalisation must be capable of expressing degrees/thresholds for properties (e.g., OBVIOUSNESS, COMPARISON, INAPPROPRIATENESS) and possibly disjunctive condition combinations that yield humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest a detailed SD model may involve a complex disjunction of conditions where each condition specifies thresholds for properties (e.g., humour occurs if COMPARISON>t1 OR INAPPROPRIATENESS>t2). Models should support graded measures rather than binary predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall combinatory question (research objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what combinations of OBVIOUSNESS, CONFLICT/COMPATIBILITY, COMPARISON, and INAPPROPRIATENESS (and possibly PREDICTION/INTERPRETATION) combine to produce humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper frames this as the central open question for IR theories: whether components can be defined using theory-external constructs or require theory-internal definitions. Solving this is a major step for humour theory and computational models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suls' residual modelling questions
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) How surprising must a portion of text be to count as a punchline? (b) What is a 'cognitive rule'? (c) Which cognitive rules produce humorous resolution vs mere patching-up of misunderstanding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit open questions raised as necessary to complete Suls' two-stage model. The paper points to 'local logic' or 'para-logic' (distorted but analogous reasoning) as a possible characterisation of cognitive rules that yield humour (see Attardo on logical mechanism).
